title: Root Mean Square Velocity of Gas Molecules
short_intro: Root mean square (RMS) velocity is the square root of the mean of the squares of the velocities of individual gas molecules. It provides a direct measure of the average translational kinetic energy of gas molecules at a given temperature.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Calculation of RMS velocity using temperature, molecular mass, pressure, and density; comparative problems involving different gases and temperatures.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation from kinetic theory postulates, relationship with Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, degrees of freedom, and translational kinetic energy per mole.

prerequisites: Postulates of kinetic theory of gases
Ideal gas equation and molar mass

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Significance
bullets: RMS velocity (v<sub>rms</sub>) is defined mathematically as v<sub>rms</sub> = √(〈v<sup>2</sup>〉).
It accounts for the directional cancellation of random molecular velocities where the vector average velocity is zero.
It is always greater than the average velocity and the most probable velocity for a given Maxwellian gas.

concept_notes.heading: Dependence on Temperature and Mass
bullets: v<sub>rms</sub> is directly proportional to the square root of absolute temperature (√T).
v<sub>rms</sub> is inversely proportional to the square root of the molar mass or molecular weight (√M).
It is independent of pressure and volume of the given mass of an ideal gas at constant temperature.

concept_notes.heading: Relation with Kinetic Energy
bullets: The translational kinetic energy per mole of an ideal gas is expressed as E = (3/2)RT.
Equating macroscopic pressure equation to molecular parameters links v<sub>rms</sub> directly to thermal energy.
At absolute zero (T = 0 K), the RMS velocity of gas molecules theoretically vanishes.

concept_notes.heading: Comparison with Other Speeds
bullets: Most probable velocity v<sub>mp</sub> : v<sub>rms</sub> : average velocity v<sub>av</sub> = √2 : √3 : √(8/π) ≈ 1.414 : 1.732 : 1.596.
The hierarchical order is always v<sub>mp</sub> < v<sub>av</sub> < v<sub>rms</sub>.
All three characteristic speeds scale linearly with √(T/M).

derivations.title: Derivation of RMS Velocity from Kinetic Theory Pressure Equation
derivations.conditions: Ideal gas, N molecules in volume V, isotropic random motion
steps: Start with the kinetic theory pressure expression: P = (1/3)(NM/V)⟨v<sup>2</sup>⟩ or P = (1/3)ρv<sub>rms</sub><sup>2</sup> where ρ is density.
Substitute PV = nRT = (N/N<sub>A</sub>)RT = NkT, where k is the Boltzmann constant.
Equate the two expressions: (1/3)(N/V)m ⟨v<sup>2</sup>⟩ = (N/V)kT, where m is the mass of a single molecule (M/N<sub>A</sub>).

derivations.title: Derivation from Law of Equipartition of Energy
derivations.conditions: Monatomic ideal gas with 3 translational degrees of freedom
steps: According to the law of equipartition of energy, each translational degree of freedom contributes (1/2)kT to the average energy of a molecule.
Total average kinetic energy of a single molecule with 3 degrees of freedom is ⟨E> = 3(&frac{1}{2}kT) = (3/2)kT.
Equate this to the microscopic kinetic energy formula: (1/2)m⟨v<sup>2</sup>⟩ = (3/2)kT.
Cancel mass and multiply by 2 to isolate ⟨v<sup>2</sup>⟩ = 3kT/m, then take the square root.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Maxwell-Boltzmann Speed Distribution Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Probability distribution curve of molecular speeds showing asymmetric bell shape with peaks for v<sub>mp</sub>, v<sub>av</sub>, and v<sub>rms</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes the fraction of molecules possessing various speeds, highlighting that v<sub>rms</sub> lies towards the higher-speed tail compared to the peak.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in PGT to identify the relative positions of the three characteristic speeds on the distribution curve.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Effect of Temperature on Speed Distribution
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two Maxwellian curves on the same axes: one at lower temperature T<sub>1</sub> (taller, narrower peak) and one at higher temperature T<sub>2</sub> (flattened, broader, shifted right).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Higher temperature broadens the distribution and shifts the RMS velocity to a higher value due to increased kinetic energy.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via conceptual multiple-choice questions regarding how peak height and RMS velocity change with heating.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Stern's Experiment / Molecular Beam Velocity Verification
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic of rotating coaxial cylinders with an oven emitting atomic beams of metal (like silver) deposited on a strip.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Directly measured the velocity distribution of atoms in a thermal vapor beam, confirming theoretical molecular speeds.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Contextual background for experimental validation of kinetic theory in advanced PGT segments.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the root mean square velocity of oxygen molecules (O<sub>2</sub>) at 27 °C. Given R = 8.31 J mol<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup> and molar mass of oxygen = 32 × 10<sup>-3</sup> kg mol<sup>-1</sup>.
solution_steps: Identify given values: T = 27 °C = 27 + 273 = 300 K, M = 32 × 10<sup>-3</sup> kg mol<sup>-1</sup>, R = 8.31 J mol<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>.
Substitute values into the formula v<sub>rms</sub> = √(3RT/M).
Calculate the square root: v<sub>rms</sub> ≈ 483.4 m s<sup>-1</sup>.

solved_numericals.question: At what temperature will the root mean square velocity of hydrogen molecules be equal to that of oxygen molecules at 300 K? Molar mass of H<sub>2</sub> = 2 g mol<sup>-1</sup>, O<sub>2</sub> = 32 g mol<sup>-1</sup>.
solution_steps: Set the RMS velocity of hydrogen equal to that of oxygen: √(3RT<sub>H</sub> / M<sub>H</sub>) = √(3RT<sub>O</sub> / M<sub>O</sub>).
Square both sides and simplify: T<sub>H</sub> / M<sub>H</sub> = T<sub>O</sub> / M<sub>O</sub>.

solved_numericals.question: If the absolute temperature of a fixed mass of an ideal gas is quadrupled, what will be the percentage increase in its root mean square velocity?
solution_steps: Initial velocity v<sub>1</sub> = √(3RT<sub>1</sub>/M) and final velocity v<sub>2</sub> = √(3R(4T<sub>1</sub>)/M) = 2 √(3RT<sub>1</sub>/M) = 2v<sub>1</sub>.
The new velocity is twice the original velocity.
Calculate percentage increase: ((v<sub>2</sub> - v<sub>1</sub>) / v<sub>1</sub>) × 100% = ((2v<sub>1</sub> - v<sub>1</sub>) / v<sub>1</sub>) × 100% = 100%.
A factor of 2 increase represents a 100% increase from the base value.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes gases obey the ideal gas law (PV = nRT), which breaks down at high pressures and low temperatures due to intermolecular forces and finite molecular volume.
Molecules are treated as point masses ignoring rotational and vibrational kinetic energy components during pure translational RMS calculations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: RMS velocity depends on the pressure of the gas container.
common_misconceptions.correct: RMS velocity is independent of pressure at constant temperature.
common_misconceptions.why: When pressure increases at constant temperature, density increases proportionally, keeping the ratio P/ρ and hence v<sub>rms</sub> constant.

common_misconceptions.wrong: All molecules in a gas sample travel at the RMS velocity.
common_misconceptions.correct: Molecules possess a continuous distribution of speeds ranging from zero to infinity.
common_misconceptions.why: v<sub>rms</sub> is only a statistical root-mean-square aggregate value, not the speed of every individual molecule.

common_misconceptions.wrong: RMS velocity and average velocity are numerically identical.
common_misconceptions.correct: v<sub>rms</sub> is always greater than the average velocity.
common_misconceptions.why: Squaring speeds before averaging heavily weights higher-speed molecules, making v<sub>rms</sub> larger than the direct arithmetic mean speed.

quick_revision: v_rms is proportional to √T and inversely proportional to √M.
RMS velocity in terms of Temperature and Molar Mass: v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}
RMS velocity in terms of Boltzmann Constant and Molecular Mass: v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3kT}{m}}
